extracted.intended_audience: government lawyers, Corps of Engineers officers, and legal advisors on navigable-waters and river-and-harbor regulation
extracted.subtask_description: A compendium of legal principles, statutory interpretations, and administrative rules governing harbor lines, obstructions, wreck removal, diversion of waters, appropriations, and enforcement under U.S. river-and-harbor and related statutes. Intended to guide officials and counsel responsible for administration and enforcement of navigable-waters law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Later treaty supersedes earlier statute when conflicting
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a later treaty (e.g., treaty of Jan. 11, 1909) is of equal obligatory force, it replaces provisions of an earlier act (e.g., act of June 29, 1906) in incidents where it conflicts; licenses issued under the earlier act expire according to their terms and future licensing is governed by the treaty (article 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: licenses under the 1906 act expire June 29, 1911; appointments and expenses under the treaty are operative and no further legislation was necessary (C. 19094, Jan. 11, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to permit diversion of water requires enabling law or alternate statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act forbidding diversion from the Niagara River (June 29, 1906), it was questionable whether the Secretary of War could authorize diversion for 'sanitary or domestic purposes' except pursuant to appropriate enabling legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, permission for necessary intake could be given under the act of March 3, 1899 pending such legislation (C. 20607, Oct. 25, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harbor lines should be located as near shore as reasonable navigation demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Harbor lines should be kept as near to the shore as the reasonable demands of navigation, present or prospective, may require because once established and structures begun in rear of them it is exceedingly difficult to move the lines farther toward the shore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy reason: to avoid later impracticability of shifting lines once reclamation and structures exist (a. 28243, Apr. 29, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary must recognize and protect littoral owners' vested rights when establishing harbor lines
rubrics_metrics.description: In establishing harbor lines the Secretary may prescribe regulations under which littoral owners (who may have property rights in flats and may wharf or dock out to navigable channel under state law) should have their vested rights recognized and protected; he may regulate budding out to the channel but cannot prohibit it, condemn, or deprive them of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit: Secretary's authority to establish harbor lines is exercised only so far as necessary for protection of the navigable channel as an interstate waterway, not to protect mere local traffic (P. 52, 211, Feb. 1892; 51, 132, Dec. 1891).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal authority to improve navigable waters extends to non-navigable-in-fact parts and supersedes state/private title to submerged lands
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States' authority to improve navigable waters is not limited to parts navigable in fact but extends to all parts of a navigable waterway so new channels may be dredged or structures prevented; any state or private title to submerged areas below high-water mark is subordinate to the U.S. authority to take and use them for navigation without compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation by the U.S. Harbor Line Board after extended inquiry may establish reasonable necessity for harbor lines (C. 28248, Apr. 29, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harbor lines may be re-established or relocated where essential to preservation and protection of harbor
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishment of harbor lines previously does not prevent the Secretary of War from re-establishing them along different lines when such action is regarded as essential to preservation and protection of the harbor.

rubrics_metrics.name: State may establish harbor lines on internal navigable waters absent federal exercise of control
rubrics_metrics.description: The river and harbor act (Aug. 11, 1888, sec. 12) did not make Secretary approval essential to a State's establishment of harbor lines on its internal navigable waters; until the United States exercises control under section 12, the State (through its municipalities) may change and regulate harbor lines without such approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to Duluth Harbor (P. 33, 308, July 1889). (VI B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict notice requirement before removal of obstructing vessels owned by private parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the river and harbor act of June 14, 1880, when the Secretary is satisfied a sunken vessel obstructs navigation he must give 30 days' notice to all persons interested in the vessel or cargo before causing removal; if the Secretary effects removal the vessel and cargo shall be sold at auction and proceeds deposited in the Treasury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the act authorizes taking private property without compensation, notice should be strictly given to all interested persons unless waived; any waiver must be definite, express, and joined in by all interested parties (P. 35, 466, Oct. 1889; C. 15140, Oct. 29, 1902). (VII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary may delegate authority to remove sunken or grounded craft to Corps of Engineers officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 20 of the act of March 3, 1899 vests authority in the Secretary 'or any agent of the United States to whom the Secretary may delegate proper authority'; thus the Secretary may legally delegate to Corps of Engineers officers in local charge the authority to remove or destroy sunken craft obstructing navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of derelict articles encountered by Engineer officers is legal and proper; give notice if property is not abandoned
rubrics_metrics.description: When derelict articles (e.g., wrecks) encountered by Engineer officers obstruct improvements required by Congress, it is legal and proper to remove them in the most effectual manner. If property is not actually abandoned and is valuable, it is generally expedient to give notice to owners (personally if practicable, or via newspapers) to remove within a reasonable time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute recognizes owner's right to remove obstructions; abandoned obstructions may be treated as property applied to removal costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 19 (act Mar. 3, 1899) is not understood to assert a U.S. property right in sunken wrecks except as arises from taking possession of abandoned property; the owner of an obstruction has the right to remove it promptly, but if he fails it will be treated as abandoned and applied pro tanto to payment of removal costs; permission may be granted to remove abandoned logs or contract for their removal provided the logs become property of the contractor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of removal may rest on negligent owner rather than the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a boat left anchored or tied was sunk by the owner's carelessness, the War Department should not remove the wreck; the burden of removal rested on the owner whose carelessness caused the sinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owners/underwriters are not statutorily obligated to remove wrecks not abandoned; abandonment calls for removal under statute
rubrics_metrics.description: When a transportation company applied for removal of its own wreck, the statute did not impose a duty upon owners or underwriters to remove where not abandoned; owners must use due precaution so vessel not be a menace, but the statute recognizes right to abandon; upon abandonment, if vessel is the menace contemplated by statute it should be removed under statutory provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: United States has no property interest in non-Government wrecks absent abandonment; cannot vest contractor with title as a contract condition
rubrics_metrics.description: When contracting for removal of wrecks not known to be fully abandoned, stipulating in the contract that removed wrecks belong to the contractor is improper because the United States has no property in such wrecks (they are not Government vessels) but only a right to remove obstructions to commerce between the States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary may dispose of sunken vessels existing >30 days at his discretion without liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 19 of Mar. 3, 1899 provides that where navigation is obstructed by a sunken vessel or similar obstruction that has existed longer than thirty days, the sunken vessel shall be subject to be broken up, removed, sold, or otherwise disposed of by the Secretary of War at his discretion without liability to owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: owner requested return of machinery after removal; recommended return upon payment of $150 removal cost (C. 7077, Sept. 22, 1899). (VII C1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Services expended to save a vessel have priority over Government's summary remedy; use admiralty proceedings to determine priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: When services and expenses were incurred in raising and repairing a vessel that had been swung free from a channel, such expenses should be regarded as having priority over the Government's claim under the statute for swinging her free; rather than resorting to the summary remedy that gives entire proceeds to Government, admiralty proceedings should be used to enforce liens and determine priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to 'bottomry bonds' priority; if owners decline vessel (elect to abandon) summary remedy may apply; if vessel sold in admiralty in foreign jurisdiction and proceeds insufficient to satisfy Government claim after payment of superior liens the Department should not retain further contract price though interest may not be payable (C. 28032, Jan. 10 & Mar. 23, 1911; Oct. 30, 1911). (VII C2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary may decline to remove wrecks that are not a menace to general navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a wreck is not a menace to general navigation but only obstructs approach to a particular company's wharves (requiring greater care in approaching), the Secretary may properly decide the wreck is not one the department is incumbent to remove under the statute and the expense of removal for the applicant's interests should be borne by the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's rules for use/navigation of U.S. canals apply to artificial works but not generally to natural waterways
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 of the river and harbor act of Aug. 18, 1894 makes it the duty of the Secretary to prescribe regulations for use and navigation of all 'canals and similar works of navigation' owned or maintained by the United States and makes violation a misdemeanor; this section does not generally apply to natural waterways even if improved and maintained by the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 424, Oct. 1894; 1047, May 1895; other cited decisions. (VIII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of obstructions to navigable capacity is prohibited; Secretary given specific authorities but enforcement lies with law officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10 of the river and harbor appropriation act (Sept. 19, 1890) prohibits creation of any obstruction not affirmatively authorized by law to the navigable capacity of waters under U.S. jurisdiction. The act invests the Secretary with specific authorities (approving bridges, giving permits for deposits, permitting erection of wharves, breaking up wrecks, establishing harbor lines), but prosecution and punishment for unauthorized obstructions are left to law officers and the courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary lacks general statutory power to remove obstructions absent appropriations or delegated authority; violations are for judicial/legal enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no law authorizing the Secretary to cause obstructions to be removed generally except as he may direct subordinates charged with river/harbor improvement where appropriations exist for the purpose; where the law is violated it is for legal and judicial authorities under sections 10 and 11 to take action by prosecution and injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstruction of navigable waters is a criminal act under section 10; federal jurisdiction displaces state authorization of obstructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 10 obstructing navigable waters of the United States becomes a criminal act; the assumption of jurisdiction by Congress displaced state authority to authorize such obstructions, and federal district attorneys should be communicated with to initiate proceedings under section 11 where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: railroad closing passage pending bridge repair prevented interstate transport; advised contacting U.S. district attorney (P. 64, 210, Mar. 1894). (IX A1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Penal environmental-dumping statutes are enforced by Department of Justice, not by Engineer Department appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of June 23, 1910 (making it unlawful to dump refuse within 8 miles of Cook County shore) imposes no duty on the Engineer Department to mark the limit or enforce the statute; penal statutes are to be enforced by bringing matters to proper U.S. attorneys and prosecuting — Engineer appropriations cannot be used for such enforcement/marking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's arrest-conferral is circumscribed; enforcement generally vested in Department of Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 17 of the act of Mar. 3, 1899 confers authority to swear processes and make arrests upon certain officers (e.g., at navy yards) for violations of specified sections, but does not empower the Secretary to authorize arrests by other officials; the general duty of enforcing the law lies with the Department of Justice and U.S. attorneys prosecute when requested by the Secretary or authorized officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary cannot, absent specific congressional authorization, ban or remove fish traps/pound nets as obstructions by regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under acts appropriating money for improvements (e.g., Columbia River), while the Secretary may make regulations for prosecution/protection of works, he is not empowered to require removal of fish traps and pound nets as obstructions by mere regulation; determining what is or may become an obstruction and ordering removal requires specific legislation from Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Congress appropriates specific sums for improvements executive must proceed to execute work without questioning expediency or delaying over title claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Congress makes an appropriation in general terms for improving a river, the executive officer charged with the improvement must proceed with the work under the appropriation without entertaining questions as to expediency of the expenditure or delaying to raise or consider claims of title to land affected by the improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'May' or 'is authorized' in river-and-harbor statutes often construed as mandatory depending on context
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissive words in river-and-harbor legislation (e.g., 'is authorized', 'it shall be lawful', 'may') are often to be regarded as equivalent to 'may' and given mandatory effect in carrying out the statute, though context can deprive 'may' of obligatory character where the statute's context indicates discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: authority to build dredge for Lake Erie treated as mandatory (C. 2473, Jan. 2, 1903); proviso about expenditure for Mobile Harbor treated as mandatory; but a clause granting discretion to 'enter into contracts for the work' was held discretionary (C. 24027, Oct. 30, 1908). (X A1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 13 (Aug. 18, 1894) on supplemental reports/estimates should be liberally construed
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 13 prohibits supplemental/additional reports or estimates for the same fiscal year unless ordered by resolution of Congress; it should be liberally construed to mean prohibition of additional estimates extending the work already estimated for and that 'resolution of Congress' includes separate resolutions of either House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proviso to an appropriation limits rather than enlarges the parent act
rubrics_metrics.description: A proviso in an appropriation is not intended to enlarge or extend the act of which it is part but to limit or restrict its language; consequently a route selection included by proviso could not be selected if owners refused to allow the free navigation provided for by the proviso.

rubrics_metrics.name: River-and-harbor work is civil, not military; Army regulations generally not applicable to civilians on such work
rubrics_metrics.description: Work done by the United States upon rivers and harbors is civil work; the fact military officers are assigned to duty does not make it military service and Army Regulations (e.g., para. 808, 1889) are not applicable to civilians employed in improvements; however Secretary has discretion to require reports mentioned in regulations where intended to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent-legislation provisos using 'may' can be mandatory as to pay/disbursement of officers engaged on work
rubrics_metrics.description: A proviso connected with permanent legislation increasing Corps of Engineers that states officers 'may' be paid from work appropriation was regarded as of permanent character and the use of 'may' in such context should be considered mandatory so that such officers when engaged must be paid from the appropriation for the work on which employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriations in same act imply disbursement under the direction of Chief of Engineers where consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriation for investigation of U.S. rights in connection with improving rivers, occurring along with other appropriations in the same act under the direction of the Secretary of War, should be disbursed by the Chief of Engineers under the general provision applying to other appropriations in that act; the Secretary may direct such disbursement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary empowered to apply appropriation 'by contract or otherwise' as most economical and may hire without formal contract for necessary purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3 of the river and harbor act of Aug. 11, 1888 makes it the duty of the Secretary to apply money appropriated 'in carrying on the various works by contract or otherwise as may be most economical and advantageous to the Government,' empowering him to authorize engineer officers to hire without formal contract when necessary for protection of levees, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractors may obstruct navigation to extent necessary for work but remain liable for unauthorized obstructions
rubrics_metrics.description: A Government contractor engaged upon river-and-harbor work may obstruct navigation to the extent necessary to do his work if such obstruction cannot reasonably be avoided; however he remains liable both civilly and criminally for any unauthorized obstruction and the Secretary of War cannot relieve him of such liability.
